\chapter{The Words That Ask, and the Word That Points Back}
\label{ch:ru-question-family}
\hlchaptermodality{22}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask who, which and how many, hang a whole clause onto a noun with kotoryy, and both ask and embed a yes-or-no question with li.}

The question family the book opened at poka closes here at seven members, all one ancient stem: kto, chto, kakoy, kak, kogda, pochemu, skolko. Two of them supply their own answers by swapping the question-stem for the pointing-stem. kotoryy is the eighth relative of the same root and the one that does the most work -- it is how a Russian noun gets described at any length. li ends the chapter by turning out to have been inside ili since the joining chapter.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kto]{\ru{кто} — \textquotedblleft{}who,\textquotedblright{} the twin of \ru{что}}

\label{lesson:RU-C22-kto}



\begin{quote}
The friend, the helping verb, and yesterday's request.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{помогать}}, and \emph{\ru{помогите}} with the polite \textbf{-\ru{ите}} on it
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{друг}}, on the root meaning \textbf{to accompany}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{надо}}, the sentence with nobody in it
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{извините}}, which literally asks to be taken \textbf{out of the guilt}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{кто}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{кто}} — \emph{kto} — \textbf{who}
\end{itemize}

Three letters, one syllable, and — unlike \textbf{\ru{что}} — it is said \textbf{exactly as it is written}. No \textbf{\ru{ш}} ambush here.

The two words are a matched pair, and Russian keeps the division sharper than English does:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{кто}} asks about \textbf{people}
  \item \textbf{\ru{что}} asks about \textbf{things}
\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{кто}?} on its own is a complete question, exactly as \textbf{\ru{что}?} is.
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{кто}} is PIE \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}is}; \textbf{\ru{что}} is PIE \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}id}. The same stem, twice, with two different endings — one for people and one for things — and the split is older than Russian, older than Latin, older than English.

Latin kept the same pair as \textbf{quis} and \textbf{quid}. English kept \textbf{who} and \textbf{what}. Russian kept \textbf{\ru{кто}} and \textbf{\ru{что}}. Three languages, one ancient distinction, none of them has ever let it go.

That is now six of the family: \textbf{\ru{как}}, \textbf{\ru{какой}}, \textbf{\ru{что}}, \textbf{\ru{почему}}, \textbf{\ru{когда}}, \textbf{\ru{кто}}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{\ru{кто}} and \emph{\ru{что}} in turn, and hear that only one of them lies about its spelling
  \item \emph{\ru{кто}?} as a whole question
  \item the six of the family in a row
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}who.\textquotedblright{} (That is \textbf{\ru{кто}}.) Which of \textbf{\ru{кто}} and \textbf{\ru{что}} is said as it is spelled? (\textbf{\ru{кто}} is; \textbf{\ru{что}} is not.) Which asks about people? (\textbf{\ru{кто}}.) Name the Latin pair that matches them. (\emph{Quis} and \emph{quid}.) And one look back: how do you ask for help? (That is \textbf{\ru{помогите}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kakóy]{\ru{какой} — \textquotedblleft{}which,\textquotedblright{} and the word the book already told you about}

\label{lesson:RU-C22-kakoy}



\begin{quote}
The verb of the heart, and two recent words.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{любить}}, English \emph{love} itself, and the \textbf{\ru{л}} that appears from nowhere in \emph{\ru{я} \ru{люблю}}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{простите}}, the heavier apology, and \emph{\ru{кто}}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{что}} hanging a whole clause under a verb, and the rule that tells \emph{\ru{извините}} from \emph{\ru{простите}}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{какой}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{какой}} — \emph{kakóy} — \textbf{which, what kind of}
\end{itemize}

You have been told about this word once before, and by a farewell. When the book took \textbf{\ru{пока}} apart it said that the old pronoun inside it became \textbf{\ru{какой}} — so the word has been named in this book for six chapters without ever being taught. It is taught now.

Look at its ending and compare it with \textbf{\ru{другой}}. The same \textbf{-\ru{ой}} does the same job in both: it turns a stem into a word that stands in front of a noun.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{какой} \ru{чай} \ru{ты} \ru{любишь}?} — \emph{kakóy chai ty lyúbish} — \textbf{which} tea do you like?
\end{itemize}

Where \textbf{\ru{что}} asks \emph{what thing}, \textbf{\ru{какой}} asks \emph{which one of these} — and it is the natural partner of \textbf{\ru{или}} when you are offering a choice out loud.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{какой}} — \emph{ka-KÓY}, stress on the end
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{какой} \ru{чай} \ru{ты} \ru{любишь}?}
  \item \emph{Build:} offer a choice with \textbf{\ru{или}}, then ask the same thing with \textbf{\ru{какой}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}which.\textquotedblright{} (That is \textbf{\ru{какой}}.) Which farewell already told you about this word? (That was \textbf{\ru{пока}}.) Which other word you own ends the same way and stands in front of a noun? (That is \textbf{\ru{другой}}.) What is the difference between \textbf{\ru{что}} and \textbf{\ru{какой}}? (\textbf{\ru{что}} asks \emph{what thing}; \textbf{\ru{какой}} asks \emph{which one}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[skólka]{\ru{сколько} — \textquotedblleft{}how many,\textquotedblright{} and the family assembled}

\label{lesson:RU-C22-skolko}



\begin{quote}
The two siblings, and two recent words.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{брат}} and \emph{\ru{сестра}}, the securest cognate pair in the book
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{медленно}}, and \emph{\ru{какой}}
  \item \emph{Recall:} how a Russian noun's ending tells you its gender
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{я} \ru{думаю}, \ru{что} …}, and \emph{\ru{повторите}} with its polite \textbf{-\ru{ите}}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{сколько}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{сколько}} — \emph{skólka} — \textbf{how many, how much}
\end{itemize}

Stress the first syllable; the final \textbf{\ru{о}} is unstressed and says \emph{a}.

English splits this question in two and makes you choose: \emph{how many} for things you can count, \emph{how much} for things you cannot. Russian does not. One word covers both, and the noun after it changes shape instead — which is a case this book has not opened, so for now keep to the question on its own.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{сколько}?} — a complete question, like the rest of the family.
\end{itemize}

The smallest answer it can take is \textbf{\ru{один}}, the number whose root became English \emph{one}, \emph{an}, \emph{a}, \emph{alone} and \emph{only}.

Its answer word is \textbf{\ru{столько}}, \textquotedblleft{}that many\textquotedblright{} — the same swap you saw when \textbf{\ru{почему}} became \textbf{\ru{потому}}: question-stem out, pointing-stem in.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — seven words, one stem}]
The whole set is now yours, and every member of it is the same ancient question-stem wearing a different ending:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{кто}} — who
  \item \textbf{\ru{что}} — what
  \item \textbf{\ru{какой}} — which
  \item \textbf{\ru{как}} — how
  \item \textbf{\ru{когда}} — when
  \item \textbf{\ru{почему}} — why
  \item \textbf{\ru{сколько}} — how many
\end{itemize}

Seven questions, one root. And two of them have pointing-word answers built by the same swap — \textbf{\ru{потому}} for \textbf{\ru{почему}}, \textbf{\ru{столько}} for \textbf{\ru{сколько}} — so the family supplies its own replies.

Learning any one of these in Russian really is most of the way to learning all of them, which is not true of the English set at all.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{\ru{сколько}} — \emph{SKÓL-ka}
  \item the seven of the family in order
  \item the two pairs — \emph{\ru{почему} / \ru{потому}}, \emph{\ru{сколько} / \ru{столько}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many English questions does \textbf{\ru{сколько}} cover? (\textbf{Two} — \emph{how many} and \emph{how much}.) How many members does the question family have now? (\textbf{Seven}.) What single move turns two of them into their own answers? (\textbf{Swapping the question-stem for the pointing-stem}.) And one look back: which word means \emph{sister}? (That is \textbf{\ru{сестра}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[katóryy]{\ru{который} — the word that hangs a sentence onto a noun}

\label{lesson:RU-C22-kotoryy}



\begin{quote}
The drink with the long journey, and the newest pattern.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{кофе}}, which travelled Arabic to Turkish to Dutch, and the letter \textbf{\ru{ф}} it needed
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{я} \ru{хочу}} with a bare infinitive after it, and \emph{\ru{сколько}}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{я} \ru{не} \ru{знаю}, \ru{что} …}, and \emph{\ru{говорите} \ru{медленно}}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{который}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{который}} — \emph{katóryy} — \textbf{who, which, that}
\end{itemize}

Four syllables, stress on the second. It is the last member of the question family, and the one that does the most work, because it does not only ask — it \textbf{joins}.

It goes back to PIE \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-teros}: the question-stem you now know well, plus an ending that means \emph{which of two}. Greek made \textbf{poteros} from it. English made \textbf{whether} — which is why \emph{whether} still means \emph{which of the two} underneath.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — a whole clause, stuck onto a noun}]
\textbf{\ru{что}} hangs a clause under a \textbf{verb}. \textbf{\ru{который}} hangs one onto a \textbf{noun}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{друг}, \ru{который} \ru{читает}} — \emph{drug, katóryy chitáyet} — the friend \textbf{who} reads.
\end{itemize}

Name a thing, put a comma, say \textbf{\ru{который}}, and say a whole sentence about it. That is how a noun in Russian gets described at any length at all, and it is the last of the joining devices this book owes you.

The comma is compulsory, as it is in front of every subordinator. English lets you drop \emph{that} — \emph{the book I read} — and Russian never does: \textbf{\ru{который}} stays, and its comma stays with it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{друг}, \ru{который} \ru{читает}}
  \item \emph{Build:} name any person you own and hang a sentence on them
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{\ru{который}} and English \emph{whether}, and hear the shared ending
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ru{который}} attach a clause to? (\textbf{A noun} — where \textbf{\ru{что}} attaches one to a verb.) May it be dropped the way English drops \emph{that}? (\textbf{No} — never, and neither may its comma.) Which English word is its cousin? (\emph{Whether}.) And one look back: which drink came by sea through three languages? (That is \textbf{\ru{кофе}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[li]{\ru{ли} — the small word that has been hiding inside \ru{или}}

\label{lesson:RU-C22-li}



\begin{quote}
The overland drink, and the word from yesterday.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{чай}}, carried west along the Silk Road while English \emph{tea} came by sea
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{который}} hanging a clause onto a noun, and \emph{\ru{или}} built from \textbf{\ru{и}} plus \textbf{\ru{ли}}
  \item \emph{Recall:} the long dash standing where the missing verb would be, and \emph{\ru{помогите}}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{\ru{вода}}, English \emph{water}, and the request pattern you have used since the first chapter
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — the doubting particle, alone}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{ли}} — \emph{li} — \textbf{whether}
\end{itemize}

You met this word six chapters ago, welded to the end of \textbf{\ru{и}}, and the book promised nothing about it then. Here it is on its own.

\textbf{\ru{ли}} does two jobs, and they are the same job seen from two sides.

\textbf{One: it makes a yes-or-no question}, without changing the word order at all. Put the word you are asking about first and \textbf{\ru{ли}} second:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{понимаешь} \ru{ли} \ru{ты}?} — \emph{panimáyesh li ty} — \textbf{do you understand?}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Two: it embeds one.} English has to swap words for this — \emph{do you understand} becomes \emph{whether you understand}. Russian does not swap anything; it uses the same \textbf{\ru{ли}}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ru{я} \ru{не} \ru{знаю}, \ru{понимаешь} \ru{ли} \ru{ты}} — \emph{ya ne znáyu, panimáyesh li ty} — I do not know \textbf{whether} you understand.
\end{itemize}

The comma is there for the same reason as everywhere else in this book: a clause is hanging under a verb.

So Russian's smallest joining word is also its question particle, and the doubt inside \textbf{\ru{или}} turns out to have been the same doubt all along.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{\ru{понимаешь} \ru{ли} \ru{ты}?}
  \item \emph{\ru{я} \ru{не} \ru{знаю}, \ru{понимаешь} \ru{ли} \ru{ты}}
  \item \emph{\ru{или}} and then \textbf{\ru{ли}} alone, and hear the piece that was always in there
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name the two jobs \textbf{\ru{ли}} does. (\textbf{It makes a yes-or-no question}, and \textbf{it embeds one as \emph{whether}}.) Which word have you been carrying it inside since the joining chapter? (That is \textbf{\ru{или}}.) Does Russian change the word order to embed a question? (\textbf{No} — the same \textbf{\ru{ли}} does both.) And one look back: which drink came overland? (That is \textbf{\ru{чай}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
